Garbled sentence in e07: 'Likewise, if you have a near-infinite amount of human-written if-then-else statements—that is, until you make a small change to the rules of the game...' is missing its main clause (presumably something like 'you can build a system that plays at superhuman level'). The notes interpret it that way.

overview.title: Chess, Deep Blue, and why fixed tasks remove the need for intelligence
overview.subsection: 19.3.3 The importance of setting the right target
overview.main_topic: The shortcut rule applied to Kaggle, to the history of AI (Newell's chess goal and Deep Blue), and to task-specific benchmarks in general
overview.central_idea: As long as AI's success metric is skill at a specific task, the field will find unintelligent shortcuts: fixing the task allows skill to be 'bought' with data or hardcoded knowledge, which removes the need to handle novelty, and therefore the need for intelligence. Collecting task-specific skills doesn't add up to general intelligence.
overview.importance: It's the book's central argument for why benchmark progress hasn't produced intelligence, and the motivation for a benchmark that measures generalization itself (ARC-AGI, p.604).
learning_objectives: Explain why Kaggle-winning models rarely reach production
Recount the story of Newell's chess goal and Deep Blue and what it taught researchers
Explain how fixing the task lets engineers 'buy' skill without increasing generalization power
Explain why there is no path from a collection of task-specific skills to general intelligence
prerequisites: The book's definition of intelligence as efficient acquisition and recombination of abstractions (p.602)

summary:
The Netflix sentence ends: the winners had **optimized for prediction accuracy alone** at the expense of inference cost, maintainability and explainability. The same holds for most Kaggle competitions: winning models rarely, if ever, go into production.

The shortcut rule has shaped AI for decades. In the 1970s, **Allen Newell**, worried that his field wasn't progressing toward a theory of cognition, proposed **chess** as AI's grand goal, reasoning that chess in humans seems to require perception, reasoning, memory and study, so a chess machine would need them too. In **1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat Kasparov**, and researchers found that a chess champion AI had taught them little about human intelligence: its search algorithm wasn't a model of the brain and didn't generalize beyond similar board games. Building a chess-only AI was easier than building a mind, so that's the shortcut taken.

More generally, *the driving success metric of AI has been to solve specific tasks*: chess, Go, MNIST, ImageNet, high school math tests, the bar exam. The field's history is a series of "successes" where *we figured out how to solve these tasks without featuring any intelligence*.

Why? Human-like intelligence isn't skill at any particular task but the **ability to adapt to novelty**, efficiently acquiring new skills for never-before-seen tasks. Fixing the task makes it possible to describe what needs to be done arbitrarily precisely, through hardcoded knowledge or huge amounts of data. Engineers can then **"buy" skill** by adding data or hardcoded rules without increasing generalization power (Figure 19.8, p.604). With near-infinite data, even nearest-neighbor search plays video games at superhuman level; with enough if-then-else rules a system can work too, until a small rule change, which a human would adapt to instantly, forces it to be rebuilt.

By fixing the task, you remove the need to handle uncertainty and novelty, and therefore the need for intelligence. Since an unintelligent solution to a specific task is always easier to find, that's the shortcut taken "100% of the time." General intelligence can produce task skills, but **there is no path from a collection of task-specific skills to general intelligence**.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The Netflix Prize winners optimized only for prediction accuracy, what they were incentivized to achieve, at the expense of inference cost, maintainability and explainability. The shortcut rule also holds in most Kaggle competitions: winning models can rarely, if ever, be used in production.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A competition leaderboard is a single metric on a fixed test set. The properties that matter in production (speed and cost per prediction, how easy the code is to update, whether people can understand the outputs) aren't on the leaderboard, so they get sacrificed for small accuracy gains, typically through large ensembles and heavy feature engineering.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It's an everyday, practical version of the shortcut rule that readers who have done Kaggle will recognize, and it prepares the much bigger claim about the whole field of AI.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: ensembles of dozens of models can gain a fraction of a percent on the leaderboard while multiplying inference cost by the same factor. In production, a team usually prefers the single simpler model.

paragraphs.excerpt: The shortcut rule has been everywhere in AI over the past few decades. In the
paragraphs.what_it_says: The shortcut rule has shaped AI for decades. In the 1970s, Allen Newell, concerned his field wasn't progressing toward a theory of cognition, proposed chess playing as AI's grand goal. The rationale: chess in humans seems to involve, perhaps require, perception, reasoning and analysis, memory and study from books, so a chess machine would have to feature them as well.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Newell's reasoning treated chess as a proxy: a task assumed to be impossible without general cognitive abilities. The hidden assumption is that the only way to play well is the human way. The rhetorical 'Right?' signals that this assumption turned out to be false.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows the shortcut rule acting on a research field: once a proxy task becomes the target, researchers optimize the task, not the abilities it was supposed to stand for.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: this is a proxy-target problem. A proxy is useful only as long as it is not optimized directly; once it is, solutions that satisfy the proxy without the underlying property appear.

terminology.meaning: Psychologist and computer scientist (1927-1992), co-creator of early AI programs such as the Logic Theorist and General Problem Solver, and of cognitive architectures.

connections: p.602: biological intelligence was the answer to a question asked by nature; chess was the wrong question

paragraphs.excerpt: Over two decades later, the dream came true: in 1997, IBM’s Deep Blue beat
paragraphs.what_it_says: Over two decades later, in 1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat Kasparov, the best player in the world. Researchers found that a chess champion AI had taught them little about human intelligence. The algorithm at the heart of Deep Blue (the book says A-star) wasn't a model of the human brain and couldn't generalize beyond similar board games. Building an AI that could only play chess was easier than building an artificial mind, so that was the shortcut taken.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Deep Blue won through massive specialized search plus handcrafted chess knowledge, evaluating on the order of hundreds of millions of positions per second. That is the opposite of the efficient recombination the book identifies with intelligence (p.602): a human grandmaster considers only a handful of candidate moves.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It's the archetypal case of a 'success' that solved the target task without the intelligence the task was meant to require.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: Deep Blue actually used alpha-beta pruned minimax search over the game tree (with custom chess hardware and a hand-tuned evaluation function), not A*. A* is a best-first path-finding algorithm. Both are search algorithms, so the book's point is unchanged. (Kasparov's first name is usually spelled 'Garry'.)

terminology.meaning: IBM's chess computer that beat world champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match in 1997.
Exploring sequences of possible moves and counter-moves to choose the move that gives the best guaranteed outcome.

connections: p.602: needing to enumerate every possible chess move is a sign of low intelligence
p.607: brute-forcing a solution space with compute is a shortcut that doesn't require intelligence

paragraphs.excerpt: So far, the driving success metric of the field of AI has been to solve
paragraphs.what_it_says: AI's driving success metric has been solving specific tasks: chess, Go, MNIST, ImageNet, high school math tests, the bar exam. So the field's history is a series of 'successes' in which we figured out how to solve these tasks without featuring any intelligence.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The list spans eras and methods: search (chess), search plus deep learning (Go), supervised deep learning (MNIST, ImageNet) and LLMs (math tests, bar exam). The claim is that each milestone was reached through the shortcut appropriate to its era, never through general intelligence. The scare quotes around 'successes' mean they are real engineering wins but not wins on intelligence.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It includes recent LLM results (exams) in the same category as Deep Blue, which is a strong position: passing the bar exam is presented as task skill, not evidence of general intelligence.
connections: p.590: ARC-AGI and LLMs' failure on novel tasks

paragraphs.excerpt: If that sounds like a surprising statement, keep in mind that human-like intelligence isn’t
paragraphs.what_it_says: Human-like intelligence isn't skill at any particular task; it's the ability to adapt to novelty, to efficiently acquire new skills and master never-before-seen tasks. Fixing the task makes it possible to describe what needs to be done arbitrarily precisely, through hardcoded human knowledge or huge amounts of data. Engineers can then 'buy' skill by adding data or hardcoded knowledge without increasing generalization power (Figure 19.8). With near-infinite training data, even nearest-neighbor search can play video games with superhuman skill. Similarly with enough human-written if-then-else rules, until a small rule change, which a human would adapt to instantly, forces the system to be retrained or rebuilt from scratch.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Skill on a fixed task comes from two sources: *information about the task* (data, rules) and *generalization power* (how far the system can go beyond that information). If the task is fixed, you can keep adding information until the task is entirely covered, and then even a system with almost no generalization power looks skilled. Nearest-neighbor search is the extreme: it generalizes only to inputs very close to stored examples, but if stored examples cover every state you'll meet, that's enough. Changing the rules shows the difference immediately, because the stored information no longer applies.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This explains the shortcut mechanically and leads directly to Figure 19.8 (p.604), where systems with different generalization power reach the same skill given enough task-specific information.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in the nearest-neighbor case, error depends on how densely the training data covers the input space. Dense coverage means a test input always has a near-identical neighbor, which is pure local generalization (p.597). The sentence about if-then-else statements in the book seems to be missing a clause, but the intent is clear: a rule-based system can be skilled until the rules of the game change.

terminology.meaning: Predicting the output for a new input by copying the output of the most similar stored training example.
How far beyond its given information (data and priors) a system can successfully operate.

connections: p.604: Figure 19.8, task-specific skill vs. task-relevant information for different generalization powers
p.597: local generalization vs. extreme generalization

paragraphs.excerpt: In short, by fixing the task, you remove the need to handle uncertainty and novelty,
paragraphs.what_it_says: By fixing the task you remove the need to handle uncertainty and novelty, and since intelligence is the ability to handle them, you remove the need for intelligence. An unintelligent solution to a specific task is always easier than solving intelligence in general, so that shortcut will be taken 100% of the time. Humans can use general intelligence to acquire skills at any new task, but there's no path in reverse from a collection of task-specific skills to general intelligence.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is a short syllogism: (1) intelligence = handling novelty; (2) a fixed task contains no novelty; (3) so a fixed task doesn't require intelligence; (4) optimizers take the easiest route; (5) so they'll find a non-intelligent solution. The last sentence denies that AGI can be reached by accumulating narrow skills one benchmark at a time.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It's the reason the book argues for a new target: measuring generalization on tasks that can't be anticipated (p.604).
connections: p.604: a new target, generalization power itself
p.616: reuse of acquired skills is necessary but not sufficient without recombination

concepts.name: Shortcut rule
concepts.definition: Optimizing a single success metric achieves it at the expense of everything the metric doesn't capture.
concepts.intuition: You get exactly what you measure, and nothing else.
concepts.technical: On this page it's applied at three scales: Kaggle competitions, Newell's chess goal, and the field's reliance on task-specific benchmarks.
concepts.significance: The argument for why benchmark progress hasn't produced intelligence.
concepts.example: Deep Blue reached the chess goal without teaching researchers about human cognition.
concepts.misconception: That a sufficiently hard task can't be shortcut. Chess was believed to need general cognition, but it didn't.

concepts.name: Task-specific skill vs. intelligence
concepts.definition: Skill is performance on a particular task; intelligence is the ability to adapt to novelty and efficiently acquire skills at never-before-seen tasks.
concepts.intuition: Skill is the output; intelligence is the machine that produces skills.
concepts.technical: On a fixed task, skill can be increased by adding task information (data, rules) without increasing generalization power.
concepts.significance: Benchmarks that measure skill can't distinguish an intelligent system from one that was given enough task information.
concepts.example: Nearest-neighbor search with near-infinite data playing video games at superhuman level.
concepts.misconception: That collecting many narrow skills eventually adds up to general intelligence; the book says there's no such path.

concepts.name: 'Buying' skill with data or hardcoded knowledge
concepts.definition: Increasing a system's skill on a fixed task by adding more training data or more human-written rules, without improving its ability to generalize.
concepts.intuition: Memorizing more answers instead of getting better at solving problems.
concepts.technical: Corresponds to moving right along one curve in Figure 19.8 (more information) rather than moving to a higher curve (more generalization power).
concepts.significance: Explains why engineering progress on benchmarks can be unlimited while intelligence stays the same.
concepts.example: A rule-based system that must be rebuilt when the rules of the game change slightly.
concepts.misconception: That a large improvement in benchmark score means improved reasoning ability.

concepts.name: Proxy task
concepts.definition: A task chosen as a target because it is believed to require some underlying capability (here, chess as a proxy for cognition).
concepts.intuition: Using a symptom to measure a cause.
concepts.technical: Once optimized directly, a proxy can be solved by methods that don't have the underlying capability.
concepts.significance: Newell's chess proposal is the book's historical example of a proxy failing under optimization.
concepts.example: Chess was thought to require perception, reasoning, memory and study.
concepts.misconception: That passing a proxy test proves the capability it was meant to stand for.

deeper.title: Why nearest neighbor can be superhuman with enough data
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, a sketch of the argument behind the claim:
1. A video game has a finite (if huge) set of game states you're likely to see.
2. If you have recorded an expert's action for nearly every state, then for any new state there's a stored state almost identical to it.
3. Copying that stored action is nearly optimal.
4. The algorithm never 'understood' anything; its skill comes entirely from the coverage of its data.
5. Change the rules (say, invert the controls) and every stored action is wrong. A human adapts in seconds; the nearest-neighbor system must collect a new dataset.

This is exactly the 'skill bought with information' the book describes.

deeper.title: The argument as a syllogism
deeper.body:
1. Intelligence is the ability to handle uncertainty and novelty.
2. Fixing the task removes uncertainty and novelty (you can specify it precisely via data or rules).
3. So a fixed task can be solved without intelligence.
4. An unintelligent, task-specific solution is always easier to find than general intelligence.
5. By the shortcut rule, it's the solution you'll get, '100% of the time.'
6. And because skills don't compose into intelligence, accumulating them doesn't lead to AGI.

deeper.title: Exam-cramming
deeper.body: A student who memorizes ten years of past exams can score highly on an exam drawn from the same pool, without understanding the subject. The exam (a fixed task) can be passed with information alone. Give the student a new kind of problem and the difference with a student who understands shows up immediately. The book uses a similar image on p.597.

misconceptions.claim: Deep Blue showed that machines can think like chess grandmasters.
misconceptions.correction: The book says Deep Blue taught researchers little about human intelligence: it relied on search, wasn't a model of the brain, and couldn't generalize to other tasks.

misconceptions.claim: Passing human exams like the bar exam shows an AI is generally intelligent.
misconceptions.correction: The book lists these exams alongside chess and ImageNet as tasks solved 'without featuring any intelligence': fixed tasks can be solved with enough data.

misconceptions.claim: If we solve enough individual tasks, general intelligence will emerge.
misconceptions.correction: 'There is no path from a collection of task-specific skills to general intelligence.'

takeaways: Competition winners optimize the leaderboard metric at the expense of cost, maintainability and explainability.
Chess was proposed as a proxy for cognition, and Deep Blue solved it without cognition.
AI's history is a series of task 'successes' that didn't involve intelligence.
On a fixed task, skill can be bought with data or rules without increasing generalization power.
Fixing the task removes the need for intelligence, and skills don't compose into general intelligence.

questions.question: Why did Allen Newell propose chess as a grand goal for AI?
questions.answer: Because chess in humans seemed to require perception, reasoning and analysis, memory and study, so he expected a chess-playing machine to need those abilities too, giving AI a path toward a theory of cognition.
questions.explanation: The page says Newell was concerned that his field wasn't progressing toward a theory of cognition.

questions.question: According to the book, what lets engineers 'buy' more skill on a fixed task without increasing generalization power?
options: Adding more data or more hardcoded knowledge
Switching to a more general architecture
Testing on tasks the creators couldn't anticipate
questions.answer: Adding more data or more hardcoded knowledge
questions.explanation: The page states this directly. Learning rates are an unrelated optimization detail; a more general architecture would address generalization, not bypass it; and testing on unanticipated tasks is the remedy the book proposes on p.604, not a way to buy skill.

questions.question: Why can a nearest-neighbor algorithm reach superhuman skill at a video game, and what exposes its lack of intelligence?
questions.answer: With near-infinite training data, any new game state has a nearly identical stored state whose action can be copied. A small change to the rules makes all stored data inapplicable; a human adapts instantly while the system must be retrained.
questions.explanation: Its skill comes from task-specific information, not generalization power.

questions.question: Explain in your own words: 'by fixing the task, you remove the need for intelligence.'
questions.answer: Intelligence is the ability to handle uncertainty and novelty. A fixed task can be described precisely in advance (by data or rules), so it contains no novelty to handle, and it can be solved without intelligence. Since that's easier, it's what will happen.
questions.explanation: This is the summary argument at the end of the page.

questions.question: Which statement matches the book's view of the relationship between skills and general intelligence?
options: General intelligence emerges once enough task-specific skills are collected
General intelligence can acquire skills, but a collection of skills doesn't lead to general intelligence
Skills and general intelligence are the same thing measured differently
questions.answer: General intelligence can acquire skills, but a collection of skills doesn't lead to general intelligence
questions.explanation: The page's last sentence. The first option is exactly what it denies; the third contradicts the skill/intelligence distinction; the fourth goes too far, since intelligence is defined as the ability to acquire skills.

questions.question: Name three properties that the Netflix Prize winners sacrificed for prediction accuracy.
questions.explanation: Listed at the top of the page.

questions.question: Pick a recent AI milestone you've heard about. Was it on a fixed task? Could its skill have been bought with data or compute? What test would show whether it reflects generalization power?
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer identifies whether the task was fixed and proposes a test with novel tasks the system's creators couldn't anticipate.
questions.explanation: This practices the book's way of evaluating claims about AI.
